title: How do we see colours?
examples: Teacher, if light hits something, what happens next?
Why do we see different colours when we look at things?
Does the colour of an object depend on the light source?

explain.say: Light is a form of energy that travels in waves. These waves carry us the energy we need to see things.
When light hits an object, the object either absorbs it or it reflects it. Reflection is what lets us see.
Our eyes have special cells called cones. These cones are what detect the different colours of reflected light.
Leaves contain a green pigment called chlorophyll. This pigment is very good at absorbing light.
Chlorophyll absorbs most colours of light, but it reflects the green light back to our eyes.

draw.text: Reflects green light back to us.

explain.say: In everyday life, think about a red apple. The apple absorbs most light and reflects the red light to your eye.

faq.q: Do we see colour because the object is actually coloured?
faq.a: No, we see colour because the object reflects certain wavelengths of light to our eyes. Different colours mean different colours of light are reflected.
asks: Where does the colour actually come from?
Is the colour inside the object?

faq.q: Does the colour change if I use a different light source?
faq.a: Yes, the colour can change depending on the light source. For example, under yellow light, everything might look a bit yellow.
asks: Does the light matter for colour?
Will it look different in sunlight?

faq.q: What is the difference between absorbing and reflecting light?
faq.a: Absorption means taking the light energy into the object. Reflection means bouncing the light energy off the surface.
asks: What happens to the light energy?
Can light be both absorbed and reflected?

faq.q: Why do some objects look black?
faq.a: Objects that look black are absorbing almost all of the light that hits them. Very little light is reflected back to our eyes.
asks: Does black mean no light is there?

faq.q: How do the cones in our eyes work?
faq.a: The cones are specialized cells in the retina of the eye. They are sensitive to different ranges of light wavelengths, which we perceive as colours.
asks: What part of the eye sees colour?

facts: Light travels in waves, and these waves carry energy.
When light hits an object, the object either absorbs or reflects the light.
The green colour of leaves comes from the pigment chlorophyll.
Chlorophyll absorbs most colours of light, but reflects green light.

quiz.say: If an object reflects only blue light, what colour will it appear to us?
quiz.why: Because the object is only bouncing blue light back to your eyes, your brain interprets it as blue.

wrong.1: This is wrong because black means almost no light is reflected, not just one colour.
wrong.2: This is wrong because white light reflects all colours, not just blue.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the colour seen depends only on the colour of light reflected.

quiz.say: What process allows us to see the colour of a red book?
quiz.why: We see the colour because the surface reflects the specific colour of light that hits it.

wrong.0: Wavelength is a property of light, not the process of seeing colour.
wrong.1: While pigments are involved, reflection is the physical process that lets us see it.
wrong.3: Absorption means the light energy goes into the object, so we would see nothing.

quiz.say: If a leaf is covered in black paint, what will happen to the light it reflects?
quiz.why: Black paint absorbs most light, so very little colour is reflected back to the eye.

wrong.0: This is wrong because reflecting all colours would make it look white.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the paint covers the chlorophyll, blocking the green reflection.
wrong.3: This is wrong because absorption takes the energy away; it does not make the object emit light.
